definition: Absolute judgment is a type of perceptual decision in which a person judges a single stimulus on its own, rather than comparing it directly with another stimulus presented at the same time or in sequence. In the source context, it refers to judging the duration of one interval, although that judgment can still be biased by stimuli or responses from previous trials.

reasons: The packet supports that the term is used for a temporal bisection/partition task with no anchor durations, but it does not define "absolute judgment" generally as judging a single stimulus on its own rather than comparing it with another stimulus.
The added contrast with stimuli presented "at the same time or in sequence" is not stated in the source and is an unsupported generalization.

The definition claims “a person judges a single stimulus on its own, rather than comparing it directly with another stimulus,” but the packet does not provide an explanation or operational distinction of absolute judgment in those terms.

While the packet clearly discusses an absolute judgment task involving judgments of temporal intervals/duration and reports carryover influences from prior response and prior interval, the “rather than comparing … presented at the same time or in sequence” component is not supported by the supplied text.
